# FX reference rates service: architecture and system design

← [Capstone brief](../README.md) · [All capstones](../../README.md)

Imports ECB euro reference rates daily, keeps the full history, and serves rates, cross rates, conversions and history with business-day fallback and attribution.

Five views of the same system, from the business context down to the cloud. Read them in order: each answers a different question that system-design interviews ask. Every diagram is provided as **Mermaid** (renders on GitHub), **draw.io / diagrams.net** XML (open and edit at [app.diagrams.net](https://app.diagrams.net)), **SVG** and **PNG**.

## 1. Solution architecture

![FX reference rates service: solution architecture](solution.svg)

**Solution architecture**: the service is the bank's single source of *reference* rates for reporting, valuation and display. The ECB is the upstream source; the US Treasury dataset is a stretch source for currencies the ECB doesn't publish (such as NGN). Dealing rates for customer trades are a separate concern.

## 2. Logical architecture

![FX reference rates service: logical architecture](logical.svg)

**Logical architecture**: an *ingestion* path (download → parse → idempotent load → cache eviction) and a *query* path (validate → resolve publication date → cross rate → round once). The store holds exactly what the ECB publishes (units per EUR); everything else is derived on read and labelled as such.

<details><summary>Mermaid source</summary>

```mermaid
%% FX reference rates service: logical architecture
flowchart LR
    subgraph sg0["Ingestion"]
        direction TB
        dl["Download<br/>(timeouts)"]
        parse["Parse CSV<br/>N/A cells · line numbers"]
        load["Idempotent load<br/>batched upsert"]
        log["Import run log"]
    end
    subgraph sg1["Query"]
        direction TB
        val["Validate codes and dates"]
        res["Resolve publication date<br/>business-day fallback"]
        calc["Cross rate / conversion<br/>10 dp HALF_EVEN, round once"]
    end
    subgraph sg2["Data"]
        direction TB
        rates[("fx_rate<br/>(currency, date) → per EUR")]
        runs[("import_run")]
        cache[("Rate cache<br/>(Caffeine)")]
    end
    dl --> parse
    parse --> load
    load --> rates
    load --> log
    log --> runs
    load -.->|"evict"| cache
    val --> res
    res --> calc
    calc -->|"lookup"| cache
    cache -.->|"miss"| rates
```

## 3. Technical architecture

![FX reference rates service: technical architecture (inside the service)](technical.svg)

**Technical architecture** shows *how the code is organised* inside the Spring Boot 4 service: thin controllers that validate and translate errors, services that hold the business rules and transaction boundaries, and a persistence layer (JPA where entity behaviour and locking help, `JdbcClient`/SQL for reporting and bulk work). Cross-cutting concerns (configuration, health, metrics, scheduling, outbound HTTP) are framework features configured once. Package by feature in code; the layers here are logical.

## 4. Infrastructure architecture

![FX reference rates service: infrastructure architecture (VPS)](infra.svg)

**Infrastructure architecture** shows *where things run* on the cheapest production-like target, a single VPS (for example SSDNodes). Only Caddy is reachable from the internet; it terminates TLS and forwards to `fx-rates-service` on Docker's internal network, so the database is never exposed (Docker port publishing bypasses `ufw`, so nothing else publishes ports). Images are built once by GitHub Actions, stored in GHCR by commit SHA, and pulled onto the server; backups leave the machine daily. Sizing and every command are in the [deployment guide](../../../deploy/README.md#3-deploy-to-a-vps).

## 5. Cloud architecture

![FX reference rates service: cloud architecture (AWS reference, Azure/GCP equivalents)](cloud.svg)

**Cloud architecture** maps the service onto managed cloud building blocks, drawn for AWS (ECS Express Mode, the AWS-recommended path for new accounts since App Runner closed to new customers in 2026). The database sits in private subnets; credentials come from the secret store, never from the image; images are immutable and tagged by commit SHA. The same design on the other clouds:

| AWS | Azure | GCP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL | Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL |
| ECS Express Mode (Fargate) | Azure Container Apps | Cloud Run |
| Amazon ECR | Azure Container Registry | Artifact Registry |
| AWS Secrets Manager | Azure Key Vault | Secret Manager |
| CloudWatch | Azure Monitor / Log Analytics | Cloud Logging & Monitoring |
| EventBridge Scheduler | Container Apps jobs | Cloud Scheduler |

Step-by-step setup for all three: [deployment guide](../../../deploy/README.md).

## Use these in your own capstone

Copy this folder into your repository, then change the diagrams to match what you actually built. In interviews, walk through the solution view first, then the logical view, then answer deep-dive questions with the technical, infrastructure and cloud views. Write a new ADR whenever you make a decision a future teammate would ask "why?" about.
